questions.question: Explain the principles of Thorndike and Kohler in learning?
questions.solution_html:
• Thorndike & Kohler Principles
  • Thorndike’s Trial and Error and Law of Effect suggest learning occurs through
  • repeated attempts and consequences. Kohler’s Insight Learning shows problem
  • solving through sudden understanding. Both explain human learning and can be
  • linked to behaviour modification in crime.
questions.final_answer: linked to behaviour modification in crime
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain the role of “mens rea” and “actus reus” in establishing criminal liability.
questions.solution_html:
• Mens Rea and Actus Reus
  • For an act to be a crime, both guilty mind (mens rea) and guilty act (actus reus)
  • must coexist. Mens rea indicates intention, while actus reus shows execution.
  • Example: murder involves intention and action together.
questions.final_answer: Example: murder involves intention and action together
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: How does the Constitutional School explain criminal tendencies through body types?
questions.solution_html:
• Constitutional School
  • Sheldon proposed body types influence personality and crime—Mesomorphs
  • (muscular) more prone to aggression, Endomorphs (soft) sociable, Ectomorphs
  • (thin) introverted. Though oversimplified, it linked biology and crime.
questions.final_answer: (thin) introverted. Though oversimplified, it linked biology and crime
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Compare and discuss Maslow’s hierarchy of needs with Herzberg’s two-factor theory.
questions.solution_html:
• Maslow vs Herzberg
  • Maslow’s hierarchy moves from physiological needs to self-actualization.
  • Herzberg divides motivators (achievement) and hygiene factors (salary). Both
  • stress motivation but differ in scope—Herzberg applies to job satisfaction.
questions.final_answer: stress motivation but differ in scope—Herzberg applies to job satisfaction
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Discuss the role of political science and economics in criminology
questions.solution_html:
• Role of Political Science & Economics
  • Political corruption, unemployment, and poverty create structural inequalities that
  • foster crime. Economic crises increase theft and fraud. Criminology uses these
  • disciplines to study macro causes of crime.
questions.final_answer: disciplines to study macro causes of crime

questions.question: Critically evaluate Sutherlands Differential Association Theory. How does it explain the process of learning criminal behaviour?
questions.solution_html:
• Differential Association Theory
  • Edwin Sutherland stated that criminal behaviour is learned through social interaction. His
  • nine propositions explain that people learn techniques and motives for crime by associating
  • with others. Frequency, duration, priority, and intensity of contacts affect learning. The theory
  • emphasized environment over heredity but ignores individual choice and innate tendencies.
questions.final_answer: emphasized environment over heredity but ignores individual choice and innate tendencies
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain in detail the conceptual difference between crime and sin. Why is a sin not always punishable under law, whereas a crime is?
questions.solution_html:
• Crime and Sin
  • Crime is a legal wrong violating state laws, punishable by court (e.g., theft, murder). Sin is a
  • moral or religious wrong violating divine law but not necessarily punishable by law (e.g.
  • lying). Thus, all crimes are sins in moral terms, but not all sins are crimes in law
questions.final_answer: lying). Thus, all crimes are sins in moral terms, but not all sins are crimes in law
